source.text:
If you have $5,000 ready to invest and no interest in picking stocks, a robo-advisor is about the simplest way to get started. You answer a short questionnaire about your goals, timeline and tolerance for risk, the platform builds a diversified portfolio of low-cost index ETFs, and it rebalances automatically from then on. For a US beginner, the decision usually narrows to the three best-known names: Betterment, Wealthfront and Schwab Intelligent Portfolios. With a starting balance this size, two things separate them more than anything else: what you pay each year and how much work the platform does to shrink your tax bill.

Start with fees, because at $5,000 the differences are bigger in percentage terms than the headline numbers suggest. Betterment's Digital plan advertises a 0.25% annual fee, but households with smaller balances (below roughly $20,000 to $25,000, depending on the tier in effect) are charged a flat fee of about $4 to $5 a month instead. On a $5,000 account, $5 a month is $60 a year, or roughly 1.2% of your balance. Wealthfront charges a flat 0.25% with no monthly minimum fee, which works out to about $12.50 a year on $5,000. Schwab Intelligent Portfolios charges no advisory fee at all; you pay only the expense ratios of the underlying ETFs.

Schwab's zero fee comes with a well-known trade-off: every portfolio holds a slice of cash, swept into Schwab Bank, and that is how the company earns money on the service. Critics call it cash drag, since money parked in cash is not working in the market. For most growth-oriented portfolios, though, Schwab's allocation rules keep that cash slice at around 2%, so on a $5,000 account the drag amounts to only a few dollars a year compared with being fully invested. The bigger hurdle with Schwab is the account minimum, which is exactly $5,000, so you clear it, just barely.

Tax features are the second half of the equation. The main one is automated tax-loss harvesting: when a holding drops in value, the software sells it to lock in a loss you can use to offset gains or a limited amount of ordinary income, then buys a similar but not identical fund so you stay invested. It has to avoid buying the same investment back within the 31-day wash sale window, or the deduction is disallowed. Harvesting only helps in taxable brokerage accounts; inside an IRA or Roth IRA it does nothing.

Betterment offers tax-loss harvesting on taxable accounts at every balance level, and its TLH+ feature coordinates between your IRA and taxable accounts so it does not accidentally trigger a wash sale by buying back a similar position in the retirement account. It is a genuinely useful design for someone who plans to hold both account types.

Wealthfront has the strongest reputation on taxes, largely because of its direct indexing, which holds individual stocks instead of an index fund so losses can be harvested company by company. The catch for beginners is that Wealthfront only turns on automated tax-loss harvesting once a taxable account reaches $100,000, so a $5,000 starter account gets automatic rebalancing but no harvesting at all. Wealthfront still has strengths at any size, including its free Path planning tool, which links to outside accounts and models questions such as when you could retire, and automated 529 college savings plans. It does not offer human advisors.

Schwab, meanwhile, makes automated tax-loss harvesting available to any taxable account that meets its $5,000 opening minimum. Schwab also simplified its lineup this year: it discontinued the Intelligent Portfolios Premium tier, the $30-a-month add-on that came with access to certified financial planners, so the service is now fully automated. Among the three, only Betterment still sells human advice, through a Premium plan that costs 0.65% and requires $100,000, which is irrelevant at this stage.

A few alternatives are worth knowing. Vanguard Digital Advisor costs roughly 0.15% a year net and needs only $100 to open, but it does not do tax-loss harvesting, so it fits best if your $5,000 is going into a Roth IRA. Subscription apps such as Acorns are easy to start with, but flat monthly fees eat into small balances much as Betterment's does.

So where should a beginner with $5,000 put the money? If fees and tax features are the priority, Schwab Intelligent Portfolios comes out ahead: no advisory fee, a small cash allocation, and tax-loss harvesting from day one. Betterment is a reasonable second choice if you value its goal-based planning tools and expect to add money quickly enough to grow past the flat-fee threshold. Wealthfront is an excellent platform, but its tax advantages are built for six-figure accounts, which makes it a better destination later than a starting point now.

Whichever you choose, the habit matters more than the platform. Set up automatic monthly deposits, decide early whether this money belongs in a taxable account or a Roth IRA, and resist the urge to check the balance every day.
